blocks.cap: Kita-ku, the night before the last, the seam over the river thin enough to read print through

blocks.p: Rei walked to the river the long way, because Gin's map said the long way was the honest one.

He went down from the flat past Jūjō Station, where the southbound platform kept its small cold patch underfoot, a weak thin spot that had been there since at least 1998 and that commuters stepped around without knowing why. He took the line one stop north to Akabane and came back on foot, because Gin had written that the drinking streets of Ichibangai were so loud with warm, ordinary feeling that two people could talk there and no Clairsentient in the ward could pick their words out. Rei did not need to talk to anyone. He needed one last stretch of noise to stand in. Then he turned south and walked toward Ōji.

Asukayama was loud. Gin had warned about that too. The old park on its hill held the Edo city in it like a smell held in cloth, three hundred years of picnics and plum blossom and executions and lovers, so dense that a reader opened to it heard a crowd where there was only grass. Not hostile, Gin had written. Just loud. Rei kept his registers closed and went past it with his head down.

Below Ōji the streets flattened out into the Kita-Ōji yards, low pre-war sheds and rail sidings and loading bays, shuttered for the festival. The Grid had never cleared the old suffering here. It lay in the corrugated walls and the oil-black ground in long untreated bands. Gin's map marked the whole district in pencil with two words. Likeliest crossing. Tonight Rei could feel why. The bands of old misery were all leaning the same way, toward the water, the way iron filings lean toward a magnet.

He came up the embankment toward the wound on the night before the last night of the festival, and the air over the river was doing the thing Higuchi's smallest, most frightened letters had warned it would do.

It was thinning the way the skin over a knuckle thins when the fist is made. Translucent and tight. The far bank was visible through a second far bank that was not there, two cities laid over one another a degree out of register.

Below him on the near bank the riverside memorial stood among its flowers, the March ground, where the grief of the eleventh came every year to settle like silt. An old woman in a flowered apron was changing the water in the vases by torchlight. She did not look up. She was speaking quietly to the river.

The paper lanterns the neighbourhood had floated an hour ago were still going downstream, little orange certainties on the black water. Behind every one of them, when Rei let his suppressed registers come halfway up, there was a second light that did not move with the current. A held breath of something on the other side, leaning close to watch the small fires the living send to guide it home.

That was the obscene thing. It was beautiful. The wall was failing and the failure looked like a festival. Rei understood at last why the Healer had chosen Obon. Not for the cover of the crowds. Because on these nights of the year the whole city has agreed to call the thinning of the wall a kindness.
Gin was already there.

He stood at the rail where the embankment path turned, in the grey cardigan he had worn all month, the one Rei could no longer look at without his throat closing. He was looking at the doubled river. Rei had learned to read his face in two layers, like everything else about him now.

Underneath was his brother. Tired and frightened and trying. The register Gin had left, surfacing the way it did when the thing wearing him eased its grip to let the body rest. Over it, calm and attentive and almost tender, was the Healer. Yushiro, the thing of Duty, the one the registry ledger would have numbered if anyone had ever caught a demon between two skins. It wore his brother's face toward the wound the way a surgeon wears a clean expression toward an open chest.

Every instrument in the CVD had read that register as stillness. Null-emotive. Filed under XIII as an absence. Only one archivist's entry, twenty-two years old and buried in Yamamoto's stacks, had ever written down the right word, and nobody upstairs had believed it. Rei had felt it in his kitchen and on his phone and across a table at the Far-Shore house, and he knew what it was now. It was not absence. It was a charge so complete that nothing else had room.
Both of them turned when they heard Rei on the gravel. Both of them, in the same body, were glad he had come. The two kinds of gladness were the worst thing he had ever had to look at.

"You found the registry," Gin said. It was the Healer's evenness in his brother's voice, and it was not a question. "I hoped you would. I left the shelf unlocked for you. The one door this whole month that did not lock itself. You noticed that. You notice everything. It is the best of you, and it is why I could never have done this with anyone else holding the other end."
He gestured at the doubled river, the lanterns, the thin bright seam where two cities almost touched. The gesture was gentle, a teacher showing a pupil the one diagram that explains the term.

"So you know what this is. You know there is a chair. You know it has stood open since the year the lights went grey. And you know, because you are the only person left alive who can feel both sides of a thing at once, that an open chair does not stay open. It only waits for the two who can close it. We are both here. The waiting is the part that is over."

blocks.cap: The counter-demon arrives on the far side of the same wound, and the trap shows its second jaw

blocks.p: Rei never had to answer. The cult answered for him.

Someone came up the far embankment, on the other side of the wound. A young man in a courier's jacket, thin as a coat hanger, walking with the loose obedient gait of a body that has been emptied and refilled. Kaito. The boy who preached in the drained pool. Kishin's mouth. Rei had hunted him through the city for days and never cornered him, and he did not arrive now as an ambush. He arrived as the second guest at an appointment.

Behind Kaito's eyes something else looked out across the water. Rei knew its weight from the Far-Shore house in Takinogawa, from the tea and the white rooms and the wall of photographs of the missing. Kishin. The despair that wore Fukai Rinka and called itself Kanna-sensei. The thing that was eating Watanabe Jun's seat out from under him and feeding toward becoming the Inverted God, the dark mirror of the Axis. It did not need to come itself tonight. It had sent its mouth to watch.
The sight of it standing across the thin bright seam from the Healer rearranged the whole month in Rei's chest at once.

They were not on the same side. They were not even the same kind of hunger. But with the river doubled between them and the lanterns burning down, Rei saw that they had been working the same wound from two ends. The Healer had thinned the wall along the grain. Kishin's Circle had cleared the room of every medium who could read what was happening. And both of them had arrived on the thin night, because whatever the chair was for, the trap had always been built for two brothers.
One of them to fill the seat. One of them to be the cost of filling it. The Healer had never needed to defeat Rei. It needed them both here, alive, on the thin night, loving each other.
"Now you see the second jaw," the Healer said. There was no triumph in it. That was the unbearable part. His brother's voice, used by the thing, was sorry.

"I told you the truth at every step, because the truth was the trap. I did not have to lie to a man who notices everything. I only had to let him notice in order. The wall thins these nights no matter what either of us does. That work is six years done. It was done before you could read a ward. What is still open is the chair, and a chair this old closes for one of two living things keyed to it. You."
He did not point at himself. He let the silence make the second name.

"Or the body I am standing in. One register goes into the seat and the office is filled and the wall is mended and the twelve stop being crushed, and Watanabe sleeps for the first time in a decade. And one register is left over, on the embankment, alive, to spend the rest of a life knowing it could have been the other way. That is the whole of it. There is no third thing across the river except the one that has come to make sure neither of us walks away from the chair. That is what the cult's friend is for. It is the lock on the door I have already opened."

Across the water Kaito smiled with a mouth that did not belong to him. It was the smile of something that wanted the chair to stay empty a little longer, and was content to watch two brothers argue over it while the wall wore thin.
Then, under the Healer's evenness, for one breath, Rei's actual brother came up.

Rei felt the register surface the way a swimmer breaks water, sudden and desperate and not given permission. Gin's hands moved before his mouth did. The right thumb pressed the left knuckles in a quick order, one, three, two, and then the heel of his hand went flat to his sternum. To anyone watching it was a tired man rubbing his hands against the river chill. Rei had read the chapter that morning. He knew a key when he saw one turned. Something on his brother's forearm under the cardigan warmed, and the Healer's grip on the tongue slipped for the length of one sentence.
Gin looked at Rei across the lanterns with his own eyes and said it fast and low, in the voice that had read to Rei when he was small.

"Rei. Don't let it be you. Whatever it says, however right it makes the arithmetic sound, the chair is the thing it wants, and it does not care which of us sits in it, and that means the one it is steering you toward is you. Let it be me. I am already most of the way gone. Let it..."

Then the Healer took the tongue back. Smooth. Unhurried. The way a man takes a pen from a child. Gin's hands went still at his sides, deliberately still, the way they had always been still when he was thinking, and the calm sorry teacher was looking at Rei again. The river ran doubled and bright between everything Rei had left to decide.
